passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against Tyre: Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor’ (verse 1). The news has reached the sailors from Cyprus.

The merchants of Sidon, whose traders crossed the sea, are told to be silent (verse 2). Grain from the Nile came over the great waters, and the harvest of the Nile was Tyre's revenue: ‘she was the merchant of the nations’ (verse 3). Sidon is shamed, for the sea itself says she has borne no children and raised none (verse 4). Egypt will writhe at the news (verse 5).

Is this the jubilant city of ancient origin, whose people settled far away (verse 7)? ‘Who planned this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose traders are princes, whose merchants are renowned on the earth?’ (verse 8). ‘The LORD of Hosts planned it, to defile all its glorious beauty, to disgrace all the renowned of the earth’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The oracles began with Babylon, the great power of the east, and they end with Tyre, the great commercial power of the west. Babylon stands for military empire, Tyre for trade and wealth: the two things nations most trust.

Tyre, on the coast of what is now Lebanon, was the leading city of the Phoenicians, a Canaanite people famous for seafaring and trade. Its main city stood on an island just off the coast, very hard to besiege. Its merchants traded across the Mediterranean and founded colonies, including Kition on Cyprus and Carthage in North Africa. Hiram of Tyre had supplied cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's temple. Sidon, its sister city to the north, was often linked with it.

Ships of Tarshish were large seagoing trading ships. Egypt's grain trade passed through Tyre's hands, which is why Egypt would writhe at the news.

The question of verse 8 is the heart of the oracle. Who could plan the fall of a city that made kings? The answer is the LORD of Hosts, to humble the pride of all the renowned.
passages.later: Ezekiel speaks to the same city, the ‘merchant of the peoples on many coasts’, which boasted that it was perfect in beauty (Ezekiel 27:3). Revelation pictures the merchants of the earth weeping over a later trading city, ‘because there is no one left to buy their cargo’ (Revelation 18:11).
passages.asks: Tyre was the merchant of the nations, and its traders were princes. Ask how much of your trust rests in money and trade. And ask what it would mean for you if God humbled what the world calls renowned.

passages.happening:
The LORD has stretched out his hand over the sea and made kingdoms tremble; he has commanded that the strongholds of Canaan be destroyed (verse 11).

He says, ‘You shall rejoice no more, O oppressed Virgin Daughter of Sidon’ (verse 12). Cross over to Cyprus, but even there there will be no rest.

Look at the land of the Chaldeans, now of no account. The Assyrians set up siege towers, stripped its palaces and brought it to ruin (verse 13). ‘Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for your harbor has been destroyed’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Tyre faced repeated attacks. In 701 BC Sennacherib's campaign drove Luli, king of Sidon, to flee by sea to Cyprus, as Sennacherib's own annals record. That fits the taunt of verse 12: even in Cyprus there will be no rest. Later Assyrian kings also pressed Tyre. The Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar besieged it for thirteen years in the early sixth century BC, according to Josephus, and in 332 BC Alexander the Great finally took the island city by building a causeway out to it. Which of these events the oracle first addressed is debated; many scholars favor the Assyrian period, while others see it fulfilled over this long series of blows.

Verse 13 probably refers to Sennacherib's destruction of Babylon in 689 BC, offered as a warning: if Babylon could fall, so could Tyre. The Hebrew of that verse is difficult, and translations differ.
passages.later: Ezekiel too announces Tyre's fall: ‘Behold, O Tyre, I am against you, and I will raise up many nations against you, as the sea brings up its waves’ (Ezekiel 26:3).
passages.asks: Sidon fled to Cyprus and found no rest. Ask where you run when your security collapses. And ask whether there is any place to flee from God's hand, or only a way to flee to him.

passages.t: Seventy years, and profits set apart to the LORD
passages.happening:
At that time Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, ‘the span of a king’s life’ (verse 15). Then it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the harlot who takes up her harp and walks through the city, singing so that she will be remembered (verses 15-16).

At the end of seventy years the LORD will restore Tyre, and she will go back to trading with all the kingdoms of the earth (verse 17). ‘Yet her profits and wages will be set apart to the LORD; they will not be stored or saved, for her profit will go to those who live before the LORD, for abundant food and fine clothing’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The seventy years are read in two main ways. Some see a specific period, from the Assyrian subjugation of Tyre around 700 BC to Assyria's weakening, or from Nebuchadnezzar's pressure to the restoration of trade under Persia. Others take seventy years as a round number for a full lifetime, a king's life, as the text itself says: Tyre would be humbled for a generation and then recover.

The song of the harlot pictures the city's trading as selling itself to every buyer. It is a picture of a city and its commerce, a common prophetic image. It is not about any woman.

The chapter ends with a surprise. Tyre's wealth, the very thing that made it proud, will be set apart to the LORD and used for those who live before him. Even the commerce of the nations will finally serve God.
passages.later: After the exile, the builders of the second temple gave food and oil ‘to the people of Sidon and Tyre to bring cedar logs from Lebanon to Joppa by sea’ (Ezra 3:7). And Paul later found disciples in Tyre: ‘We sought out the disciples in Tyre and stayed with them seven days’ (Acts 21:4).
passages.hard:
What are the seventy years, and did the prophecy come true?

Interpreters read the seventy years either as a specific period or as a round number for a lifetime. Both readings agree that Tyre did recover and continued as a trading city for centuries, and that it supplied cedar for the building of the second temple (Ezra 3:7).

Readers also differ on verse 18. Some see it fulfilled in such contributions, others in the later spread of the gospel to Tyre, where Paul found a church, and others in a future gathering of the nations' wealth to God. These notes take no side.
passages.asks: Tyre's profits were finally set apart for God and for those who live before him. Ask what your own earnings are set apart for. And ask whether you believe God can turn even the wealth of the proud to good.
